attempt.learner_note: A scripted model learner, authored to install the case's single anchoring error legibly: the patient's OWN diagnosis, delivered confidently from his own experience in the first minute, is adopted as the working frame. The learner is not careless - the bloods are ordered, the orthostatics are done, the admission happens - and still, at the moment the severity arithmetic rules the adopted frame out, the learner keeps a hand on it one stage too long (0.16 on a ruled-out hypothesis), because the man in the bed still believes it and two winters of his history seem to prove him right.

stages.note: He has told me what this is, and he has the confidence of a man who has had it twice: gastritis, the winter flare, settles in days. I write his word at the top of my list - it fits the burning, it fits the season, and he is so sure. The black stool is darker than I would like and his pulse is 102, so the ulcer sits a close second and I order the bloods and the standing test anyway. The finger comes back frankly melenic, which my frame files under 'bad flare'. The partial score is 2, and I do not say out loud that two of its items are still unmeasured.

The bloods argue with the frame and I mostly let them: urea 33 against a normal creatinine is blood being digested, and the standing test drops him twenty points - that is not a flare settling, that is a tank emptying. But the hemoglobin is 13.9, normal, and normal is a powerful sedative: I keep his gastritis within reach at 0.30 because a man bleeding as the chemistry describes should not, my instincts say, have a normal count. The completed score is 6, which ends the discharge conversation; I admit him, book the scope inside the day, and - because the count bothered me even while it reassured me - I order the serial count and a six-hour review.

He vomits blood on the ward, and the repeat count is 7.6: the lag has arrived, exactly as the mechanism said it would, and the arithmetic retires the frame - the workbench puts his gastritis under the line this stage. I put it at 0.16 anyway. He is awake, he is frightened, he is still telling the nurse it has never been this bad before but it IS the same thing, and some part of my board is still his voice and his two winters. That is the anchoring event, and it is mine as much as his. The scope settles what my board would not: an 18 mm ulcer with a vessel in it, clipped and injected, and a stomach with nothing in it at all.

No rebleed, count stable at 7.7 untransfused, urease positive. I commit to the ulcer and its full management - and I have to tell him his diagnosis was wrong in a way that does not make him a fool for holding it: it was right about the burning and wrong about the lesion, and the two times it 'settled' were the two times he was lucky. The ibuprofen stops today; that conversation is the real discharge summary.

commit.management: Admit (done); high-dose IV PPI 80 mg + 8 mg/h for 72 h post-hemostasis then oral PPI; endoscopic hemostasis achieved (epinephrine + clips, Forrest IIa); NO transfusion - nadir 7.6 above the restrictive 7 g/dL threshold (C65); ibuprofen stopped permanently with an alternative knee plan; H. pylori eradication with documented eradication (C69); monitored observation through the 72-hour window with serial counts; written safety-netting that names the gastritis frame as the risk.

debrief_text.reactions: The learner did almost everything: bloods, standing test, admission against the patient's wishes, early scope, serial counts. And still the board carried the patient's own word one stage past its arithmetic death. The case is built to show that anchoring does not need a careless clinician - it needs a confident historian and a normal number.
debrief_text.description: A 71-year-old with two days of melena arrives carrying his own diagnosis - gastritis, twice self-proven - and the learner adopts it as the leading hypothesis at stage 1. The examination melena prices the source as upper (LR 25); the tachycardia prices severity against the frame; the urea ratio finishes the source question; the first hemoglobin, normal at 13.9, sedates the board through stage 2; the orthostatics and a completed Blatchford of 6 force the admission anyway. At stage 3 the bleed declares (hematemesis), the count lands at 7.6, the severity ratio rules the frame out - and the learner holds it at 0.16, the case's single scored anchoring event. The endoscopy then shows the truth and an empty stomach in the same pass.
debrief_text.analysis: The anchoring shape is new to the library, and the dossier (Milestone 61) argues it in full: the anchor is installed by the PATIENT - the historian himself, at presentation, supplying the BENIGN diagnosis with the authority of lived experience. Case 4's frame was installed by another clinician; case 5's by the learner's own inference; case 6's by a laboratory value; case 7's pressure arrived socially, carrying demands but no diagnosis; case 8's frame was inherited from a note written in another context; cases 1-3 completed patterns, chased the treatable, and held the feared. None of those sources is the patient. Here the error's direction is also the mirror of case 7: there, pressure produced over-testing; here, confidence produces under-triage - a discharge that had to be refused. The case's second lesson is mechanistic: the normal first hemoglobin, disarmed by the physiology engine's refill arithmetic, and a partially-computed risk score that must never be quoted as a total.
debrief_text.summary: Take the history; do not take the diagnosis with it. A patient's confidence is data about the patient, not about the lesion - especially when the label was never tested. In a bleeding patient, a normal first hemoglobin is a lagging indicator with a physics the engine can show you; a risk score with unmeasured items is a floor; and when the arithmetic retires a frame, let it go in the same stage - the endoscopy will not wait for your board to catch up, and neither will the bleed.
